name: Gàlì
confidence_why: no confirmed first-hand statement: the record's source was not confirmed
catalog_citation: Jungraithmayr, Herrmann & Carsten Peust. 2019. Notes on Gàlì (Miltu), a moribund Chadic language (Republic of Chad). Folia Orientalia 56: 219-230. DOI 10.24425/for.2019.130711
catalog_locator: sec. 2.1.3 'Tone', p. 222 (PDF p. 4 of 12; saved file the copy we hold)
catalog_quote: The language has been recorded with three tone levels: à low, ā mid, á high. In addition, two contour tones have been observed: ǎ low-high, â high-low. While the number of contrastive tones cannot be considered as definitive, there is no doubt that Gali is a tone language, as is a priori expected for any Chadic language. Illustrative minimal pairs are: nǝ̀ “we” ≠ nǝ́ “I”; pààṛ “blood” ≠ pááṛ “sun”; tǝ̀ṛ “man” ≠ tǝ́ṛ “moon”.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gali/Miltu is described as a lexical tone language (three levels plus two contours, provisional); the only existing linguistic description says nothing at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; authors caution the number of contrastive tones is not definitive (data from a one-day visit, 24 March 1972)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on words in isolation/short phrases from 1972 field notes (~40 nouns, verbs, numerals, pronouns). No stress domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Jungraithmayr & Peust describe the language under its autonym Gàlì (people Gàlìɲ), spoken in Miltou village on the Chari, = Glottolog milt1241 / ISO mlj 'Miltu'. They note a possible dialect Dǝmraw upriver; Roberts 2021 shows that variety (Boor, boor1242) is a distinct language (38-51% lexical similarity), so the statement applies to Miltu proper only.

Sec. 2.1 Phonology covers consonants, vowels and tone only; sec. 2.1.3 (p.222) says Gali is a tone language with three recorded levels (L, M, H) plus LH and HL contours, with minimal pairs. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent and read).
